title: Thief mails 460 million-yen watch back to Tokyo store he stole it from, says “I’m sorry”
description: Latest crook to hit Tokyo’s hottest theft target feels either remorse or fear, but probably shouldn’t expect forgiveness. In a city as big as Tokyo, different neighborhoods have different atmospheres, but those reputations can change over time. For example, Nakano is best known for its Nakano Broadway shopping center, which used to be thought of […]
content:
Latest crook to hit Tokyo’s hottest theft target feels either remorse or fear, but probably shouldn’t expect forgiveness.

In a city as big as Tokyo, different neighborhoods have different atmospheres, but those reputations can change over time. For example, Nakano is best known for its Nakano Broadway shopping center, which used to be thought of almost entirely as a place for fans of eclectic pop and subculture genres, sort of like a weirder, less trendy version of Akihabara. Over the last few years, though, Nakano Broadway has become famous for having a dense concentration of luxury wristwatch stores, stocked with both new and used high-demand models.

Sadly, Nakano Broadway’s reputation is continuing to evolve, and it’s now becoming a place known for attracting not only watch fans, but watch thieves too. On the evening of October 29, a man, at the time seemingly an interested shopper, approached a salesperson inside a watch store in Nakano Broadway and asked if he could try on a piece that was in a locked showcase. The salesperson obliged, and the man slipped on a watch from Swiss brand Audemars Piguet, only to suddenly run off with it still on his wrist. And while the man hadn’t been an actual shopper, he apparently still knew a thing or two about watches, as the model he stole has a price of 46 million yen (approximately US$290,000).

▼ A CG reenactment of the crime

After fleeing the building, the man escaped out into the web of narrow streets that twist around Nakano Broadway. However, this is still a fairly developed part of Tokyo, not the sort of place where a sprinting thief can blend in with fitness joggers, but Nakano also isn’t so dense one can easily disappear into a sea of passersby either. As a result, investigators were able to spot the fleeing man in recording from multiple security cameras, as shown in the video here.

▼ The video also shows the model of watch that was stolen.

Though the thief is still at large (as of this writing), the stolen watch has been returned, and, surprisingly, it was the thief himself who returned it, via a takuhaibin/parcel delivery service. On the morning of November 1, a cardboard box which had been mailed from Aichi Prefecture was delivered to the store that was robbed, and when the staff opened it, they found a watch matching the model and serial number of the one that was stolen, plus a handwritten letter of apology that included the statement “I’m sorry.” The watch doesn’t appear to have suffered any noticeable damage during its time away from the store.

Online reactions to the unexpected turn of events have included:

“Must have realized it was only a matter of time until they caught him.”
“Okay, so he got spooked and returned the watch. He still stole it.”
“Returning it doesn’t undo the crime. Turn yourself in.”
“It’s like he thinks they’ll just treat it as a prank since he the watch back.”
“If you know you should return it, you should have known not to take it in the first place.”
“Thieves have totally marked Nakano Broadway.”
“If they’re going to let people try on watches that are that expensive, they should make them do it in a locked room.”

With law-abiding citizens in Japan still fuming over a different brazen watch robbery that recently took place at Nakano Broadway, it’s not surprising that public sentiment isn’t leaning towards letting the guy off the hook just because he returned the property that he stole. Japan is, after all, the country that says “If everything could be solved by saying ‘sorry,’ we wouldn’t need police,” and investigators are still searching for the thief.

title: This is Japan’s best cycling course, but is it fun for bicycling beginners too?
description: We head to the Seto Inland Sea for a Shimanami Kaido sampler. Japan has a lot of great places for bicycling, but the Shimanami Kaido Cycling Road is widely considered to be the best. Stretching across the Seto Inland Sea, the 70-kilometer (43.5-mile) route ties together seven different islands as it runs from the town […]
content:
We head to the Seto Inland Sea for a Shimanami Kaido sampler.

Japan has a lot of great places for bicycling, but the Shimanami Kaido Cycling Road is widely considered to be the best. Stretching across the Seto Inland Sea, the 70-kilometer (43.5-mile) route ties together seven different islands as it runs from the town of Imabari in Ehime Prefecture on Shikoku all the way to Onomichi, Hiroshima Prefecture on Japan’s main island of Honshu.

But while the idea of a 70-kilomter, possibly multi-day ride sounds fun for dedicated cyclists, is it possible for beginner-level bicyclists to enjoy the Shimanami Kaido too, even if they can’t devote a whole day to it? That was the question our Japanese-language reporter Saya Togashi found herself asking. Saya lives in a fairly rural part of Japan, and the lack of public transportation means that she spends pretty much every day getting around by car. Sure, she knows how to ride a bike, but it’s not something she does very often, and certainly not to the extent that she’s built up a fitness cyclist’s musculature and stamina.

And yet, Saya could still feel the Shimanami Kaido calling to her, and her initial research suggested that while the course is loved by serious cyclists, it’s very accommodating to novices as well. For starters, there are 10 official rental cycle depots along the route, so there’s no need to bring your own bike. Depending on the type of bike and specific location, some of the depots even allow you to drop off your bike at a different spot than where you started your ride, in case you want to go part-way across the islands on bike, then do the rest by car, bus, or boat.

Saya decided to get her bike at the Imabari Itoyama Rental Cycle depot in Imabari, essentially the southernmost tip of the Shimanami Kaido. It’s possible (and, honestly, advisable) to reserve a bike ahead of time, but Saya hadn’t made any such arrangements. Nevertheless, when she showed up at around 10 a.m. on a weekday, they still had plenty of bikes available, even some electric-assist ones like the one Saya picked out, which cost 4,000 yen (US$25) for one day.

▼ Imabari Itoyama Rental Cycle also provides helmets free of charge.

Instead of the full-course Shimanami Kaido, Saya’s plan was to experience the first section, sort of an appetizer-size version. Since Imabari Itoyama Rental Cycle has a free parking lot, she could leave her car there while she was pedaling and take her time without worrying about racking up expensive parking fees.

After Saya selected her bike, the staff adjusted the seat height for her and pointed her towards the nearby bridge that makes up the start of the course. They also explained that you can tell when you’re following the Shimanami Kaido by the blue lines marked on the pavement, so there’s no fear of getting lost.

This first bridge, called the Kurushima Kaikyo Bridge, is less than 10 minutes from the rental cycle depot, and it’s a very big piece of infrastructure, about 50 meters (164 feet) up above the shoreline. The bike path, though, spirals around on the way up to keep the incline from getting all that steep, and especially if you’re using an electric-assist bike, it’s not so strenuous, even for a beginner like Saya.

The high guard rails were also reassuring, keeping Saya and her bike separated from car traffic on one side and safe from the drop-off down to the sea on the other. The peace of mind they provided left Saya with the necessary mental space to appreciate just how beautiful the view is from up here.

The weather was a little cloudy on this day, but that added to the atmosphere, and also meant the sun wasn’t beating down on her with full force. There are so many islands in this part of Japan that sometimes they look like they’re layered on top of one another. On the closer ones Saya could make out individual houses and other buildings, while the ones farther in the distance, wrapped in a light mist, looked like they could be part of an ink seascape painting.

Though she’d worked up a bit of a sweat, Saya was making steady progress, and had a smile on her face with no stress in her heart. She felt like she’d sprouted wings as she smoothly zoomed ahead to the far side of the bridge…

…though she stopped for a bit at a cyclist rest area, not because she was worn out, but to snap a few more photos and bask in the cool sea breeze for a bit.

Once you come down on the other side of the bridge, you’re still in Imabari City, but now on the island of Oshima, in a picturesque coastal community.

Following the blue line in the road brought Saya to Yoshiumi Ikiiki Hall, the island’s michi no eki/”roadside station,” a center for local foods and handicrafts. Bringing her bike to stop and heading into the food court, Saya spotted several other cyclists who were biking the Shimanami Kaido in whole or in part, and she decided to fuel up with a fish sandwich, a sausage one…

…and, of course, some soft serve ice cream.

This was as far as Saya was planning to ride today, but rather than rushing straight back to Imabari Itoyama Rental Cycle, she stopped by the Oshima port along the way, which offers short sightseeing cruises on the Seto Inland Sea.

In total, Saya covered around six kilometers on her round-trip ride from the rental cycle depot over to Oshima and back, and spent around an hour and a half pedaling. This is, she admits, only a very small portion of the Shimanami Kaido, but she still feels like it was enough to understand what makes the course so fun. In addition to experienced bicycling buffs doing the whole thing, she also saw people like herself who were clearly just doing a part of it. She saw people of different ages and backgrounds, and even from different countries, all enjoying this unique activity, creating a heartwarming sense of comradery, and at one point when she got off her bike to readjust the seat, a passing cyclist stopped to make sure she wasn’t in any sort of mechanical distress.

So yes, Saya is happy to report that you don’t have to go hard-core to enjoy going along part of the Shimanami Kaido. Maybe she’ll eventually cycle the whole thing, broken up into different segments on different trips, but if and when she, or you, are ready to go all the way from one end to the other, we’ve got a report on what that’s like too.

title: Mr. Sato searches for the mysterious new wall of fortune in Tokyo
description: Our new favorite hole in the wall. Our reporter Mr. Sato discovered one such spot not too far from him in […]
content:
Our new favorite hole in the wall.

Every city has a few mystery spots here and there where something is created and left for others to discover, but the reason why is sometimes only known to the people who did it. Our reporter Mr. Sato discovered one such spot not too far from him in Tokyo’s Shibuya neighborhood, where there’s been some buzz on social media about a wall that gives you your fortune.

After some online research, Mr. Sato found the location of this wall of fortune called “Kabe Uranai” and set out to see it in person.

The wall is located in the Miyamasuzaka area of Shibuya, but it’s a little tucked away. According to Mr. Sato, you have to take the exit from Shibuya Station heading for Miyamasuzaka and walk up the slope. When you see an Excelsior Caffe on the corner, turn right. From there you’ll see a restaurant called Steak Rice no Mise that has “Japanese Steak Bowl” written on the sign in English.

I suppose we could give you a map, but there should be some element of adventure when seeking out a mysterious fortune-telling wall.

The wall is just to the right of the steakhouse, and it’s rather easy to miss. Although it is slightly different from its surrounding wall, it’s very unassuming, with what looks like an ordinary electrical box connected to it.

However, that box is actually the control panel for Kabe Uranai.

Inside is a terminal that you can use to purchase your fortune. It costs 999 yen (US$6.30), and the wall accepts credit card, QR code payment, and other digital payment services, but does not accept cash. Mr. Sato was able to use his Suica prepaid card here.

On the inside of the door were instructions explaining that if you pay the money and touch the wall, you’ll receive a pack of fortune cards with instructions to follow. As you can see, the wall of fortune has full English guidance so even people from other countries can enjoy it.

After paying the money, Mr. Sato placed his hand on the wall…

Suddenly, it made a rumbling sound and the stone began to move!

Underneath it was his treasure: a pack of fortune cards bathed in a golden beam of light.

It was all pretty exciting and made Mr. Sato feel like Indiana Jones for a moment. He took his cards and the stone slid back into place.

Inside each pack are nine cards. The first two are instructions, and the other seven are randomly selected. Mr. Sato won’t spoil the surprise, but they’re kind of a mix between fortune-telling and sending you to certain places in the area.

Regardless of where Mr. Sato’s cards took him, the whole experience was very fun, and he’d recommend it to anyone in the area. And for those not in the area, it appears that Kabe Uranai walls will be appearing elsewhere too. One is scheduled to open in Ikebukuro in November, Nagoya in December, and Osaka in 2027.

Who knows where one will appear after that? You’d need some kind of fortune-telling wall to figure that out.

title: Starbucks Japan releases now Tokyo Reserve Roastery Christmas drinkware collection [Photos]

content:
Starbucks Japan’s premium brand is ready to help you get started on Christmas shopping right now.

Starbucks Japan didn’t waste much time transitioning from Halloween scares to the Christmas spirit, as it began serving up its new Frappuccino with optional Christmas cooking toppings on November 2. And for those looking to get an early start on their Christmas shopping, searching for presents either for other or themselves, the Starbucks Reserve Roastery Tokyo is now offering a new line of holiday-season drinkware.

As a reminder, the Reserve Roasteries, like the one pictured above in Tokyo’s Nakameguro neighborhood, are Starbucks’ locations for premium celebrations of coffee culture, and the holiday season collection is a similar combination of fancy and festive design, with a theme of “Decorate your holiday season” and glittery pearl motifs, such as with this 355-milliliter (12-ounce) stainless steel drink bottle that looks like it’s all dreseed up for a Christmas party with a pearl necklace-style strap.

If you’re looking for something with a little more capacity, there’s a more conventionally-shaped 473-milliliter drink bottle that’s still sparkly, as is the identical-volume cold cup tumbler.

Moving on to drinkware for your at-home coffee/tea breaks, Japan doesn’t really have a Christmas tradition of hanging stocking over the fireplace, due in no small part to fireplaces not really being a thing in Japanese homes. Instead, you’ll see “Christmas boots” in holiday decoration displays here, and also as the inspiration for this 237-milliliter mug.

Equally cozy, but a little larger for longer beverage breaks, is the 355-milliliter “Harvest White” design…

…and if you want to be fancy without going out, there’s a “Pink and Copper” mug too.

This 296-milliliter icy blue drinking glass might look more all-purpose wintery than specifically Christmas-y, but its double-wall design makes it versatile in handling both hot and cold drinks.

There’s a little more visual warmth in the color palate for the pair of 355-mililiter stemmed glasses, whose shape are modeled after the coffee bean silo seen inside the Starbucks Reserve Roastery Tokyo.

And eventually Starbucks Japan’s theming wraps back around on itself, as the Christmas decoration-inspired drinkware inspires a Christmas tree ornament shaped like the boot mug, plus one modeled after the Christmas packaging of the Reserve Roastery’s coffee and coffee press, and a glittery snow globe.

And finally, there are a pair of bag charms, one chic and one playful…

…and a selection of corduroy drawstring pouches, in two sizes and three colors.

As for price, the necklace-style strap drink bottle is the priciest item, at 7,200 yen (US$45), followed by the non-strap bottle (5,900 yen) and tumbler (5,300 yen). The mugs are all 3,600 yen, the double-wall glass 4,000, and the stemmed glasses 3,300 each. The ornaments are each 2,300 yen, the snow globe 3,800, the bag charms 4,800 each, and the bags 1,300 or 1,600 each, depending on size.

In addition to in-store at the Starbucks Reserve Roastery Tokyo, the lineup is also available through the Starbucks Japan online store here.

title: Japanese government announces criteria for creating backup capital of Japan
description: Four cities are the most likely candidates to become vice-capitals in case Tokyo is struck by an incapacitating natural disaster. Over the course of history, Japan has had several capital cities. Most famously, the imperial court was previously located in Kyoto, and before that in Nara. There was also a period of around 150 years […]
content:
Four cities are the most likely candidates to become vice-capitals in case Tokyo is struck by an incapacitating natural disaster.

Over the course of history, Japan has had several capital cities. Most famously, the imperial court was previously located in Kyoto, and before that in Nara. There was also a period of around 150 years when Kamakura, by nature of being the then-ruling shogunate’s base of power, operated as the de-facto capital.

In 1868, though, the capital was moved to Edo, resulting in the entire city being renamed Tokyo, which literally means “eastern capital.” And while Tokyo isn’t in danger or losing that status, the Japanese government has now decided on a set of criteria for cities that want to become Japan’s official backup capital.

The idea of designating a fukushuto (literally “vice-capital”) has been one that proponents have been kicking around for a while. Initially it was spearheaded by the Nippon Ishin (Japan Innovation) Party, a political group with a great deal of influence in Osaka, Japan’s third-largest city by population. The purposed purpose would be to have a backup plan in place in the event of a natural disaster in the Tokyo area, such as a large earthquake or eruption of Mt. Fuji, rendering government institutions in Tokyo unable to function.

▼ Osaka’s reputation for making superior takoyaki (octopus balls) compared to Tokyo, while not explicitly stated, was no doubt seen as an important factor as well.

Seeking support from a potential coalition with Nippon Isshin voters, Japan’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party also began putting its weight behind the idea, and after agreeing to move forward with the initiative last summer, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s cabinet has now released a set of criteria for cities applying for backup capital status.

To qualify, the backup capital city must be located within a prefecture that contains at least 1.2 percent of Japan’s total population and accounts for at least 2.1 percent of the nation’s GDP. It must also be located sufficiently far enough from Tokyo to be outside the area of effect of any disaster that would incapacitate the current capital, and it must also have facilities for at least half of the 28 classifications of national government field offices.

The distance-from-Tokyo requirement eliminates the city of Yokohama, since despite being Japan’s second-largest city, it’s only about 30 minutes south of the capital, so any natural disaster causing significant damage to one is likely to hit the other hard as well. However, despite Osaka politicians having been the ones who got the ball rolling on this whole vice-capital idea, they now seem to have rivals for that designation. In addition to Osaka, Aichi, Fukuoka, and Hokkaido also meet the cabinet’s criteria, and it is suggested that those prefectures’ legislators will make a push for the cities of Nagoya, Fukuoka, and Sapporo, respectively, to be chosen as a backup capital, though the current framework of the ordinance doesn’t explicitly prohibit multiple cities from being awarded the status.

It’s worth noting that, according to the Japanese government’s National Personnel Authority, there are more than 40,000 government employees working in Tokyo’s Kasumigaseki district, where the majority of the city’s government facilities are located. While the vice-capital initiative doesn’t call for a complete 1:1 backup for every single office and worker, it would, as a matter of course, require some level of redundancy, and the related hiring and infrastructure development, funded by tax revenue, could represent a significant economic windfall for any city chosen as a vice-capital, and also give local legislators substantially more political clout. There’s also the question of whether debating and choosing backup capital cities is the most effective use of politicians’ time and energy, considering that rising costs of living, stagnating wages, and crime are probably more immediate concerns for the vast majority of ordinary citizens and residents of Japan.

The cabinet is expected to spend the next year or so drafting the fundamental policies for how the vice-capital site would operate, which is slated to be presented next October prior to official site selections.

title: This hot spring near Osaka’s Kansai Airport resolves the pick-two-out-of-three bathhouse dilemma
description: Perfect for when you’ve got to fly, but want to soak. Generally, when it comes to hot springs in Japan, you can pick two of the following three things: convenient location, beautiful view, and not crowded. Someplace with a convenient location and nice scenery? Be prepared to share the tub with a whole lot of […]
content:
Perfect for when you’ve got to fly, but want to soak.

Generally, when it comes to hot springs in Japan, you can pick two of the following three things: convenient location, beautiful view, and not crowded. Someplace with a convenient location and nice scenery? Be prepared to share the tub with a whole lot of other people. Great view and small crowds? Probably going to have to be some small, hidden place way off the beaten path. Centrally located but not crowded? Odds are it’s because the ambiance isn’t that impressive.

But it turns out sometimes you can have it all, like we did on our recent visit to Senshu no Yu.

▼ Natural Hot Spring Senshu no Yu (天然温泉 泉州の湯)

Senshu is the old name for the Osaka region, and yes, Senshu no Yu is located within Osaka Prefecture. As a matter of fact, it’s located very close to Kansai International Airport, central Japan’s largest air travel hub. Kansai International is on an island that’s connected to the mainland by the Sky Gate Bride R, and as soon as you get across it, siting right there is Senshu no Yu.

The bathhouse is about a 10-minute walk from Rinku Town Station on the Nankai Airport Line/JR Kansai Airport Line, which is itself only a six-minute ride from the airport, so this is a very convenient location is you’re looking to enjoy a hot spring bath as soon as possible after arriving in Japan, or maybe to indulge in one more right before you fly home. As for the view, it’s quite beautiful, with both the glass-in indoor and open-air baths giving you expansive lines of sight out across the bay.

OK, so this place has to be packed, right?

Let’s head on in from the first-floor entrance, up to the lobby on the second floor, and…

…huh.

It’s not like the interior is run-down or short on amenities, either. Everything was invitingly clean, from the tatami-floor relaxation space with shelves of manga to read to the cafe. If you want something more substantial to eat, there’s also a restaurant…

…with a nice, chill vibe and more great views.

OK…so is this place super pricey? Nope. Weekday admission is 900 yen (US$5.65), and on weekends and holidays they charge 1,000. If you didn’t bring your own towel, hand towels can be rented for 100 yen, and bath towels for 200.

▼ Entrance to the baths

Senshu no Yu was even chosen among the country’s top 30 scenic-view hot springs by users of Japanese Internet portal Nifty.

So what’s the catch? We’re not entirely sure, but it might have something to do with what most travelers think of when they hear “Osaka.” Osaka City is Japan’s third-largest city by population, and brings to mind the bustling streets of the Dotonbori canal district and its huge selection of shops and restaurants. Senshu no Yu, though located inside Osaka Prefecture, is in the town of Izumisano, which is way on the southern outskirts of Osaka City.

Downtown Osaka is about an hour by train to the northeast of Senshu no Yu, and there’s not much in the way of sightseeing attractions in any other direction once you get across the bridge from the airport. The result is that most people just zoom right past the neighborhood without ever realizing why it’s worth making a special stop in.

It should be noted that there is a hotel next door to Senshu no Yu, and with more and more travelers coming to Japan, it might not have its hidden-in-plain-view status for long. For now, though, it’s a rare chance to enjoy a hot spring soak without having to compromise on convenience, ambiance, or crowdedness.

title: Starbucks Japan invites us to par-tea with its new Earl Gray Frappuccino [Taste test]
description: Three new drinks, featuring seven kinds of tea, join the Starbucks Japan menu. This year’s Halloween parties are over and done with, but that doesn’t mean the fun is over for sweets fans. On November 2, Starbucks Japan rolled out no fewer than three new sweetly soothing beverages, and we rushed out to try them […]
content:
Three new drinks, featuring seven kinds of tea, join the Starbucks Japan menu.

This year’s Halloween parties are over and done with, but that doesn’t mean the fun is over for sweets fans. On November 2, Starbucks Japan rolled out no fewer than three new sweetly soothing beverages, and we rushed out to try them all.

“Let’s par-tea” is the theme of this new lineup which aims to please lovers of puns and black tea, and while all three of them looked very tempting, we felt the strongest allure from Starbucks Japan’s newest Frappuccino, the Earl Grey Chocolate Frappuccino.

By pouring a bunch of chocolate chips into an Earl Grey tea base, Starbucks has created something that appeals to a sophisticated sweet tooth, especially with the partnering presences of chocolate sauce and a swirl of whipped cream on top. And since Japan starts getting into the Christmas mood right after Halloween, you can dress up your 690-yen (US$4.30) Earl Grey Chocolate Frappuccino with a Christmas cookie for an additional 70 yen.

The bright-colored Christmas present-shaped confectionary made for a cheery visual accent against the dark color of the Frappuccino itself, and while the combination looked so pretty we almost felt bad about drinking it, that hesitation only lasted until the moment it fired up our taste receptors. Our resident Frappuccino expert K. Masami handled taste-testing duties, and says that the elegantly aromatic sensation of Earl Grey tea arrives first, creating a serenely relaxing mood. The sweetness of the chocolate chips come next, but it blends smoothly with the tea notes while adding in some crunchy texture. As you continue to sip, or swirl your straw around, more of the chocolate sauce gets drawn into the mix, upping the sweetness but without becoming unpleasantly cloying, especially with the whipped cream helping to smooth together the various component flavors.

Up next: the Joyful Medley Strawberry Creamy Tea Latte.

This 650-yen latte features Starbucks Joyful Medley holiday tea mixture of black tea, oolong tea, and jasmine tea, plus a touch of apricot flavor. Beloved by fans for its complex taste that nonetheless comes to a clean finish, the Joyful Medley is joined for this drink by fresh cream, strawberry mouse, and a sprinkling of freeze-dried strawberry bits across the top.

Our Joyful Medley Strawberry Creamy Tea Latte was also joined by the optional cookie topping, and this time we got a Christmas tree (there’s also a possible Santa hat cookie, adding a bit of a gacha element).

Once again, this is a beautiful drink to look at, but tastes too good to spend very much time only visually admiring. The comforting blend of teas, rich creaminess, and sweetly tart strawberry flavors were so good together that Masami almost stopped sipping to give the drink a round of gleeful applause, and she especially recommends it to Starbucks fans who look forward to the Joyful Medley blend every year as a fresh new way to enjoy the blend.

And finally, Masami checked out Starbucks Japan’s new Royal Milk Tea (620 yen). An original blend of Darjeeling, Assam and Ceylon tea, this one might not be as inventive as the other drinks we taste-tested here, but it’s still very satisfying, especially in your order your hot on a chilly autumn evening.

All three drinks are listed as limited-time items, and since Starbucks Japan tends to get very busy with rapidly releasing new items as we get closer to the end of the year, it’s probably best to have your tea par-tea as soon as you can.

title: Tokyo Skytree set to offer breathtaking Diamond Fuji natural phenomenon view this month
description: The Tokyo landmark is a perfect spot on an ancient ley line of spiritual power to view the sight of Mt. Fuji with a diamond of light on its summit. Twice per year around February and November, anyone close enough to see Mt. Fuji can witness Diamond Fuji, a natural phenomenon when the rising or […]
content:
The Tokyo landmark is a perfect spot on an ancient ley line of spiritual power to view the sight of Mt. Fuji with a diamond of light on its summit.

Twice per year around February and November, anyone close enough to see Mt. Fuji can witness Diamond Fuji, a natural phenomenon when the rising or setting sun aligns perfectly with the mountain’s peak. When the conditions are just right, the sun’s rays then pan outward, giving the appearance of a shining diamond ring nestled on top of Japan’s highest mountain. This stunning phenomenon is next predicted to happen on November 8 around 4:30 p.m.

▼ The view of Diamond Fuji in November 2025

While any relatively tall spot in the Greater Tokyo Area is prime viewing to catch a glimpse of Diamond Fuji, the Tokyo Skytree‘s two main viewing platforms–the Observation Deck at 350 meters (1,1448 feet) high and the Observation Galleria at 450 meters high–have a special claim to fame as to why Diamond Fuji is best viewed from one of them.

▼ Crowds gathered at the Tokyo Skytree Observation Deck at the Diamond Fuji phenomenon in February 2026

As described on the Tokyo Skytree’s website, the landmark was actually constructed on a kind of spiritual pathway that links several significant sites in the Kanto region:

“Tokyo Skytree is built on a ‘ley line,’ a straight line connecting ancient ruins and sacred sites such as Mt. Fuji, Meiji Jingu Shrine, the Imperial Palace (formerly Edo Castle), and Kashima Jingu Shrine (Kashima City, Ibaraki Prefecture), and is said to be a place where positive energy gathers.”

Therefore, by viewing Diamond Fuji from a location on this line, tradition says that you can essentially charge yourself with plenty of positive energy for the months to come–similar to visiting one of Japan’s various “power spots.”

▼ Highlighted locations from left to right: Mt. Fuji, Meiji Shrine, Imperial Palace, Tokyo Skytree, and Kashima Shrine

Regular Tokyo Skytree entrance fees apply for viewing the Diamond Fuji phenomenon on November 8. Viewing conditions are also unpredictable depending on the weather conditions, so please be prepared in advance. title: Japan ends tax-free shopping system for foreign tourists, new refund request system now in effect
description: What to be aware of as Japan tightens the rules for tourists saving 10 percent on their purchases. As of November 1, Japan has ended its tax-free shopping system for foreign tourists. Up until now, non-residents making purchases in Japan could avoid paying sales tax when shopping at participating stores by showing their passport as […]
content:
What to be aware of as Japan tightens the rules for tourists saving 10 percent on their purchases.

As of November 1, Japan has ended its tax-free shopping system for foreign tourists. Up until now, non-residents making purchases in Japan could avoid paying sales tax when shopping at participating stores by showing their passport as long as their total purchase price came to 5,000 yen (US$31.50) or more. As sales tax in Japan is generally 10 percent, and most major retailers, as well as a great many smaller ones, offered this service, overseas visitors to Japan were able to save a considerable amount of money, especially with shopping having become an especially popular activity for foreign tourists benefiting from the weak yen.

The tax-free arrangement has now been replaced by a tax-refund system. Foreign tourists will now be required to pay sales tax in full at the time of purchase, and then apply for the amount to be refunded prior to their departure flight from Japan.

Under the new system, travelers will still need to show their passport when purchasing items at retailers. Then, at the airport or seaport that you’re leaving Japan from, you’ll need to complete a tax refund application process at a kiosk or electronic self-service terminal. After showing your passport, the customs agent or terminal screen will inform you whether or not your application requires an additional inspection, and if it does, you’ll need to show all of the items that you’re seeking a tax refund for. In other words, you’ll need to complete the application process, and the inspection too, if required, before checking in your luggage.

▼ Self-service terminals will display either a green or red notice after you present your passport.

Maps showing the locations of the terminals and inspection areas inside Japan’s major airports can be found online here.

▼ Terminal and inspection areas (marked in blue) inside Haneda Airport’s Terminal 2, International Flights Area (3rd floor)

▼ Haneda Airport Terminal 3 (3rd floor)

In addition, travelers departing from Narita, Haneda, Kansai, Chubu Centrair International Airport, Fukuoka, New Chitose, and Naha airports can perform the application online through the Visit Japan Web website. However, doing so requires being connecting to a dedicated Wi‑Fi network for the procedure within the international departure lobby, so you’ll need to be at the airport either way.

Once the procedure is complete, you can designate whether you wish to receive your refund via your credit card company or a bank transfer. The Japan Customs website does not mention a timeframe for refund processing, but a few weeks is likely, so you’ll want to make sure you’re not counting on that money for anything critical like rent or groceries.

▼ Narita International Airport Terminal 1 (4th floor)

▼ Narita International Airport Terminal 2 (3rd floor)

So what prompted this change? Well, Japan’s sales tax is technically a “consumption tax,” and proponents of waiving it for foreign tourists figure that if the items aren’t going to be used/consumed in Japan, there’s no need to levy a tax on those purchases, which makes prices lower for tourists and helps boost sales for retailers. Japan’s tax-exemption system was basically operating on the honor system in that regard, though, which left the door open for dishonorable types to pass off or resell the tax-free items within the country. Changing to a tax refund system gives customs officials a way to confirm that the items really are going to be taken out of Japan before the purchasing tourist benefits from the untaxed price, and while not all travelers requesting a refund will be subject to inspection, it’s probavbly something you should be prepared for if you’ve done a lot of shopping during your trip.

Something to be careful about regarding the tax refund system is that all items purchased at the same time (i.e. on the same receipt) are counted as a single, unbreakable unit. So, for example, if you purchase five items at the same time, and you get flagged for an inspection, you have to be able to present all five of those items to qualify for the tax refund for that purchase. If you’re missing even one, you won’t be eligible for a refund for the other four item, either. Likewise, if you purchase, say, multiple bottles of skincare lotion and opened one of them to use during your time in Japan, you won’t be able to claim a refund for the others unless they were purchased as a separate transaction/on a separate receipt. In addition, tax refund requests must be made within 90 days of an item’s purchase, though since 90 days is the standard tourist visa length for international visitors to Japan, this won’t be an issue for most shoppers.

▼ Narita International Airport Terminal 3 (2nd floor)

Finally, under the new regulations it is the traveler’s responsibility to complete the procedure within time to check in for their flight. If you don’t, there’s no framework for requesting refunds at a later date, so if you stand to get a lot back, you’ll want to make sure to get to the airport early, though with the system being brand-new, there are not yet any official guidelines as to how long the procedure will take.

title: Japan’s mini Shikoku Pilgrimage walking tour left us feeling immensely satisfied
description: The full pilgrimage takes weeks to complete, but if you’ve got a couple hours, this Matsuyama experience will show you what makes the tradition so special. The Shikoku Pilgrimage route is, unquestionably, a great Japan travel experience. After all, people have been walking it, tracing the footsteps of famed Buddhist monk Kukai (also known as […]
content:
The full pilgrimage takes weeks to complete, but if you’ve got a couple hours, this Matsuyama experience will show you what makes the tradition so special.

The Shikoku Pilgrimage route is, unquestionably, a great Japan travel experience. After all, people have been walking it, tracing the footsteps of famed Buddhist monk Kukai (also known as Kobo Daishi), for 1,200 years now.

However, the full route, which goes all around the island of Shikoku, is also a very time-consuming travel experience, taking roughly six weeks if you do it on foot. Odds are you don’t have that much time, and neither did we on our recent visit to the Shikoku city of Matsuyama in Ehime Prefecture. What we could fit into our itinerary, though, was a 90-minute Pilgrimage Experience Guided Walk which takes you to one of the 88 temples along the route, with guidance in traditional pilgrimage customs along the way.

We and the other participants gathered at the pre-arranged meeting point on Matsuyama’s Dogo Shopping Street, not far from the city’s famous Dogo Onsen hot spring bathhouse. There we met our guide, who provided each of us with a sleeveless hakue, the white cloth tunic worn by Shikoku pilgrims, a sugegasa (conical straw hat), and kongozue (walking stick).

▼ There’s no mask that’s part of the outfit, that’s just a little privacy mark.

As you might remember from the glowing review from our ace reporter Mr. Sato, Japanese straw hats are surprisingly comfortable, since not only do they keep the sun off of you, their construction means they don’t sit directly on top of your head like a baseball cap or other Western-style hats, providing better air circulation and to help keep you cool, all good things when you’re walking to and from temples.

There’s a more morbid reason for the white tunics, though. The Shikoku Pilgrimage doesn’t present any grave dangers in the modern era, but centuries ago, when you couldn’t just whip out your phone and call for help if you became sick, injured, or lost, embarking on the route carried the risk that you might not make it back home. In Buddhist funeral rites, the body of the deceased is wrapped in a white garment prior to cremation, and the Shikoku pilgrimage tunic is white so that if someone were to meet with an untimely death along the way, they would already by properly dressed for cremation.

But, to be clear, you won’t be on any mortal danger as part of this guided mini-pilgrimage, in which you walk from Dogo Onsen to Ishiteji Temple, the 51st of the 88 temples on the pilgrimage route. It takes about 20 minutes to reach the temple, and along the way we spotted such quant aspects of the neighborhood as haiku mailboxes in which anyone can submit a haiku poem they’ve written, from which a committee selects the best works every three months for awards. We also saw numerous ashiyu open-air foot baths filled with hot spring water, as well as a statue of Matsuyama-born master haiku poet Masaoka Shiki reflecting his other great passion, baseball.

▼ The guy was also pretty fond of sweet bean bread.

As our group progressed further away from the bustling Dogo Shopping Street, we noticed local residents politely greeting us. “Good morning,” one would say, followed by another encouraging us with “Hang in there.” We asked our guide is these were friends or acquaintances acknowledging us by extension of their relationship with him, but he told us no, he’d never met these specific residents. With the pilgrimage route being such an important part of Shikoku culture, residents have made a custom of showing warmhearted respect to those walking the route, either in whole or part.

We then reached Ishiteji Temple, where we learned another unique part of Shikoku culture.

Soon after entering the temple grounds, we came to a stone bridge, and our guide instructed us to be careful not to tap our walking sticks on it as we crossed. This sort of specific prohibition isn’t the norm at temples in Japan, but as the guide explained, it’s connected to Kukai. When he was doing the very first Shikoku Pilgrimage back in the ninth century, Japan didn’t exactly have a robust leisure hotel industry. Sure, there were scattered inns here and there, but a lot of times Kukai didn’t have a roof over his head when he had to make camp for the night, and so he’d often sleep underneath bridges. Because of that, pilgrims should avoid hitting the upper surface of bridges with their walking sticks, as a metaphorical show of respect and consideration to the monk who might have been sleeping below.

Ishiteji has two halls, where we lit candles and incense. Again, our guide gentle reminded us of the importance of consideration for others on the pilgrimage route, recommending that we place our lit offerings at the highest, farthest back, and most laterally centralized positions, so that those who came after us could place there’s without having to pass their hands over our flames.

After that, we took a short rest and munched on some roasted mochi, a specialty of the temple that pilgrims have been enjoying for generations, and sipped a cup of green tea, which are offered as a set for 600 yen (US$3.80).

As with a lot of temple visits and activities in Japan, the Pilgrimage Experience Guided Walk isn’t presented with an atmosphere of severe solemnity, nor as something only for individuals of markedly devout Buddhist faith, and can be participated in and enjoyed as a cultural experience rather than a strictly religious one. That said, there’s something special about knowing you’re helping keep a tradition alive more than a millennium after it started, and the kind greetings we received from townspeople along the way put us in a contemplative but happy mood that stayed with us long after we were back where we’d started in Dogo. We may have only completed one eighty-eighth of the Shikoku Pilgrimage, but we still felt completely satisfied with the part of it we’d seen this day, and if you’d like to try it for yourself, reservations can be made through the website of tour provider Matsuyama Haiku here.

title: Beautiful Ghibli diorama kits lets you build anime characters’ homes inside yours [Photos]
description: Papercraft models are small in size, but colossally cool for fans of Studio Ghibli. content:
Papercraft models are small in size, but colossally cool for fans of Studio Ghibli.

Earlier in the year Ghibli Park added a new exhibit consisting of over 30 large dioramas made by famed anime director Hayao Miyazaki. Odds are, though, that you don’t have that much space to devote to your love of Ghibli’s art and environments, but Japanese papercraft company Sankei does have a way to let you bring a little piece of the Ghibli world into your home.

Going on sale November 3 are three new entries in Sankei’s Miniatuart Mini Plus line, recreating locations from Howl’s Moving Castle, Kiki’s Delivery Service, and Arrietty.

Each of them starts as a box filled with sheets of paper from which to build the walls and interior, and after you assemble everything the box then becomes a stand for the completed diorama.

Though the scale is compact and the building materials simple, the kits contain an incredible level of charming detail. Howl’s hearth, for example, is cluttered with all sorts of magical baubles and reference materials, just as you’d expect the eccentric wizard’s living quarters to be, and even fire spirit Calcifer makes an appearance.

The room that Kiki and Jiji rent from bakery owner Osono is decidedly less chaotic, but still has a lived-in feel with the witch’s laundry hanging up to dry, her broom leaning against the windowsill, and Jiji making sure not to leave any dirty pawprints on the nice clean floor.

The Kiki’s kit also has the most detailed exterior, which really helps create the atmosphere of it being a miniaturized loft that scaled-down version of the characters could live inside.

▼ The kits’ boxes/bases bear different illustrations on different sides, too, giving you one more reason to view them from different angles

Rounding out the trio is Arietty’s family’s living room.

This one comes with an extra dash of coolness because the scale of the diorama (6 centimeters [2.4 inches] square) works as a reminder that Arietty and her kin are all so tiny that most of the humans whose house they lived inside of never noticed them.

All of the locations are filled with cozy vibes, but they are listed on Sankei’s website as being advanced-difficulty kits, with an estimated time of five hours or more to build Kiki’s room, and 10 hours or more for the others. Kiki’s kit is also the lowest-priced of the bunch at 4,290 yen (US$27), followed by Arrietty’s (6,160 yen) and Howl’s (6,600 yen). All three can be ordered starting November 3 through Sankei’s Rakuten online storefront (here, here, and here).

title: Shoplifting prevention guard arrested for shoplifting boot from store he was guarding
description: Those boots weren’t made for walking away with. In tough economic times, where even stores are switching to automated checkouts to save money, it’s no surprise that incidents of shoplifting have been steadily rising in Japan. To combat this, some retailers have employed what are known as “manbiki G-men,” plainclothes security guards whose role is […]
content:
Those boots weren’t made for walking away with.

In tough economic times, where even stores are switching to automated checkouts to save money, it’s no surprise that incidents of shoplifting have been steadily rising in Japan. To combat this, some retailers have employed what are known as “manbiki G-men,” plainclothes security guards whose role is to patrol stores and prevent sticky-fingered shoppers.

Although the name is a throwback to prohibition-era FBI agents in the USA, these guards have no government authority like the police. Instead, they keep an eye on shoppers, shadow anyone suspected of shoplifting until they leave the store without paying, and then make a citizen’s arrest.

But having manbiki G-men watch shoppers begs the question of who is watching the manbiki G-men. The answer to that question has revealed itself recently at a home improvement store in Hiroshima Prefecture on 27 October. 

▼ The incident occurred at the Home Plaza Nafco in the picturesque town of Sera.

At about 11 a.m. on that morning, a plainclothes police officer spotted the plainclothes security guard taking a single rubber boot, concealing it in his clothing, and attempting to take it from the store without paying. It was later revealed that the man is actually employed by the same store as a manbiki G-man, but it is unclear if he was on duty at the time of the incident.

About a month prior to this, the store had contacted police about an uptick in shoplifting there, which put them on high alert. After being arrested on-site by the plainclothes police officer, the 66-year-old suspect admitted to the crime, saying he stole the single boot because he needed it.

Though with a tragically ironic twist, it was an open-and-shut case. Once again, a man’s desire for a single rubber boot corrupted him to the point of abusing the power entrusted to him by his employer.

“It’s always darkest right under the lighthouse.”
“I guess they need some manbiki G-men G-men.”
“Maybe he was just trying to get inside the head of his target.”
“Are they not even paying their G-men enough to get some rubber boots?”
“We’re not going to make it, are we? The country, I mean.”
“You either die a G-man or live long enough to become a shoplifter.”
“Fascinating! It’s like the end of a Poirot story.”
“I wonder if he just needed one boot or was planning to make two trips.”

Regardless of whether or not he really did need a second piece of footwear, we can be certain the home improvement store will be figuratively giving him the boot. Hopefully, he was just caught up in the thrill and excitement of stealing some Wellies, because that’s at least slightly less bleak than an employed person being unable to afford a pair on his own.

So, let that be a lesson to all you junior G-men out there. While bustin’ two-bit flimflammers, it can be right tempting to get yer mitts on some cabbage for yourself too, but the only easy street that lands you on leads straight to the hoosegow.

title: Pokémon guitars from Fender Japan come with 8-bit sound mode for covering retro game music [Vid]

content:
Fender celebrates Red and Green’s 30th anniversary with guitars saluting the Pokémon world in both looks and sound.

In the English-speaking world, the start of the Pokémon video game series were the paired releases of Pokémon Red and Blue for the Game Boy in 1998. However, unbeknownst to many young fans at the time, the real origins of the franchise had come out in Japan two years prior, and were titled Pokémon Red and Green.

Here in 2026, the global Poké-fan community has a more comprehensive picture of the franchise’s history, which brings us to the appropriate color schemes for the latest collaboration celebrating Pokémon’s 30th anniversary, a pair of customized guitars created in partnership with Fender Japan.

In a parallel to how mainline Pokémon games customarily have a similar but still different sibling, so too has Fender chosen two different models of guitar for this team-up, the Made in Japan Pokémon “Red Version” Stratocaster and Made in Japan Pokémon “Green Version” Telecaster.

Within the series’ visual design language, the color red is often associated with Fire-type Pocket Monsters, and green with Grass-types, so the body of each guitar is covered in pixel art of species from those categories.

More fan-service flair can be found on the neck, where Poké Balls are subtly scattered about…

…and the backside features a Pokémon 30th anniversary plate.

In addition to their visual salutes to the Pokémon world, these made-in-Japan guitars make an audio one too.

Push in the volume knob, and you can activate what Fender has dubbed the instruments’ “8-Bit Sound System Mode,” a clever audio effect that gives the guitar’s sound a quality reminiscent of nostalgic chiptunes, which should lend itself really well to playing covers of classic Pokémon games’ soundtracks.

▼ A demonstration video of the 8-Bit Sound System Mode

Each guitar also comes bundled with a selection of pixel art picks, plus a custom hardcase and certificate of authenticity.

Because they’ll be available in limited quantities, both guitars, priced at 396,000 yen (US$2,490) each, will be offered for sale through a lottery system from the Pokémon Center Online store, which will be accepting applications between noon on November 19 and 4:59 p.m. on November 24 (Japan time).

title: This semi-secret, totally free footbath in downtown Tokyo is completely awesome
description: The Museum of Narratives has an oasis for your feet. They say there’s no such thing as a free lunch, but it turns out there is a free foot bath in Tokyo. It’s not some rinky-dink little tub in some obscure spot on the outskirts of the capital, either, but right in the middle of […]
content:
The Museum of Narratives has an oasis for your feet.

They say there’s no such thing as a free lunch, but it turns out there is a free foot bath in Tokyo. It’s not some rinky-dink little tub in some obscure spot on the outskirts of the capital, either, but right in the middle of downtown, near Takanawa Gateway Station on the Yamanote train line that encircles the city center.

Takanawa Gateway is the newest station on the line, and is connected to a shopping, entertainment, and cultural development called Takanawa Gateway City, part of which is MoN Takanawa: The Museum of Narratives.

The museum, which opened in March, hosts rotating artistic and cultural events, but on our visit, we didn’t need to purchase a ticket, because we weren’t heading inside the main exhibition areas. Instead, our destination was someplace on the sixth-floor, an exterior area that many people aren’t aware of called the Ashiyu Terrace. Ashiyu is the Japanese word for “footbath,” and that’s exactly what you’ll find here!

This outdoor urban oasis has an outer ring of greenery, and beyond that offers impressively open views of the surrounding cityscape, of a kind that’s not easy to come by this deep in downtown without going to a skyscraper’s upper floors.

This is thanks to the terrace’s position adjacent to the train tracks, plus Takanawa Gateway’s proximity to the next station to the south, Shinagawa. Shinagawa is one of Japan’s densest rail hubs, and the seven different lines that converge there each need their own amount of space as they approach the station, creating a rare broad, low patch in downtown Tokyo’s urban topography that creates wide lines of sight.

▼ This also makes the MoN Takanawa footbath a great place for trainspotting rail fans.

Because the foot bath is open-air, it’s probably not the most pleasant place to spend a blisteringly hot summer day or a frigidly cold winter evening. Right now, though, on a fall afternoon, the weather is perfect for this sort of thing, especially since in addition to a cozy-warm hot water area…

…the Ashiyu Terrace also has a cold water area.

This means you can start off in the warm section until you’re feeling nice and toasty, and once you get a little too hot, you can mosey on over to the other end of the bath and cool down. Then, if you’re anything like us, you’ll eventually migrate back to the warm section, and repeat the process a couple more times before you’re ready to leave this ankle-deep aquatic paradise.

If you’re looking for more ways to enjoy traditional Japanese culture on the free-to-access museum grounds, there’s a little Shinto shrine on the rooftop…

…and a tatami reed-floor relaxation room on the fourth floor with digital art displays, which is also free to access.

▼ The tatami mats are new enough that they still have a very noticeable relaxing earthy fragrance.

Really, the only possibly negative thing we could say about the Ashiyu Terrace is that no towels are provided, but we’re happy to bring our own handkerchief to dry off with when the rest of this experience is this awesome.

title: Japan’s TeamLab digital art group is opening a permanent museum in America
description: Internationally acclaimed art collective will have a new home not far from Disneyland. Japan’s TeamLab has risen from relative obscurity to become one of the most admired digital art collectives in the world, using their technological wizardry and ethereally emotional sensibilities to craft experiences unlike those from anyone else. Their exhibits and museums regularly top […]
content:
Internationally acclaimed art collective will have a new home not far from Disneyland.

Japan’s TeamLab has risen from relative obscurity to become one of the most admired digital art collectives in the world, using their technological wizardry and ethereally emotional sensibilities to craft experiences unlike those from anyone else. Their exhibits and museums regularly top lists of must-visit places for artistically inclined travelers in Japan, but now it’s time for TeamLab itself to embark on an overseas journey, as it’s announced that it will be opening its very first permanent museum in the U.S.

Sunny southern California is where TeamLab will be setting up in the States. The group’s facility will be part of the city of Anaheim’s currently in-development OCVIBE cultural, entertainment, and sports complex, which will also have green spaces, offices, hotels, and apartments.

▼ Examples of the sort of art that TeamLab creates

TeamLab Museum Anaheim is the tentative name of the facility, but it won’t be a shock if they eventually decide on something with a little more pizazz, seeing as how their museums in Japan have creative names such as TeamLab Borderless or TeamLab Planets. The Anaheim museum is planned to have a total floor space of roughly 10,000 square meters (approximately 110,000 square feet).

▼ A preview image showing TeamLab Museum Anaheim, with its shimmery sea green exterior, connected by a pedestrian bridge to the Anaheim Regional Transportation Intermodal Center rail station, with Angel Stadium behind it on the opposite side of the 57 Freeway

In announcing the Anaheim museum, TeamLab co-founder and director Toshiyuki Inoko said:

“I am filled with happiness that we will be opening TeamLab’s first large-scale museum in America at OCVIBE in Anaheim. Through art, TeamLab seeks to explore the nature of consciousness and existence. Our exhibits change through the existence of people, with visitors themselves becoming part of the piece. By becoming immersed in the artwork, visitors are connected, without boundaries, to both the installation and the world. By gathering and placing ourselves alongside others in this location where sports, music, and culture intersect, we will come to perceive the world in new ways and share those perceptions with others.”

OCVIBE is planned to open in phases, with the first coming in the spring of next year and featuring an amphitheater, restaurants, and park. TeamLab’s museum, though, is projected to open in 2030, but fans will tell you that the group’s creations are worth the wait, and that’s still two years earlier than the projected opening of its new Tokyo museum.

title: Can Japan’s Self-Defense Forces legally open fire on a zombie horde?
description: This legal discussion contains scenes of explicit violence and gore. It’s Halloween again, and what better way to ring in the spookiest of holidays than with some thought exercises on complex constitutional law issues. Although most zombie stories focus on a ragtag group of civilians coping with civilization collapsing all around them, the beginning of […]
content:
This legal discussion contains scenes of explicit violence and gore.

It’s Halloween again, and what better way to ring in the spookiest of holidays than with some thought exercises on complex constitutional law issues. Although most zombie stories focus on a ragtag group of civilians coping with civilization collapsing all around them, the beginning of the outbreak usually shows the military going all out in trying to eliminate the undead threat.

And with many of these movies and TV shows taking place in the USA, it’s no surprise to see the armed forces meeting the waves of zombies with guns blazing. In Japan, however, such a response is not so simple. While most countries’ militaries operate on a principle of “anything shy of a war crime is fair game,” Japan’s Self-Defense Forces operate in the opposite way and require very strict conditions before they can perform a certain action.

A good crash course in this can be found in our analysis on how the military can legally deal with a kaiju attack. Long story short, it is possible if Godzilla is classified as a “natural disaster” and the weapons used against him are classified as “tools” to neutralize the threat to Japan.

Zombies are much more complicated, however. Although certain aspects of the Godzilla scenario can be applied here, the fact that the threat is or was human introduces bigger legal hurdles for military and police forces. A video recently posted in the Legal Insight series by Tonari no Bengoshi Hosokyoku looks at this situation in-depth, but while their legal knowledge is spot-on, I’m concerned with some of their zombie awareness.

To start, much like with Godzilla, the SDF can be dispatched in a disaster relief capacity without issue. This means they can organize evacuations, set up barricades for shelters, and act in cases of self-defense to protect the public, just like police do. However, in this capacity, they cannot launch an assault on the zombies. One exception would be if the zombies were unleashed on Japan by a foreign government. This is the same reason that Godzilla cannot be considered an enemy combatant but King Ghidorah (sent by those jerks on Planet X) can.

So, let’s say our zombies are homegrown from some virus or mushrooms or something. Now, the question is whether they are people or not. According to Legal Insight, if they are classified as living people, then killing them can be considered murder, but even if they’re dead, filling them full of lead is also the crime of desecrating human remains.

However, Legal Insight also says that a zombie would be legally declared a corpse, and thus considered an “object” rather than a “person.” In this case, they could be treated in a way similar to wild animals that pose a threat to human life and be dealt with by the Self-Defense Forces using their  guns as “tools,” much like with Godzilla. The desecration of a corpse charges would be outweighed by the need to protect lives, much like how scuttling an abandoned ship adrift in the ocean is deemed necessary despite the destruction of property involved.

But I think that’s where they got it wrong.

Despite all of our advances, humans are still not great at determining if something is alive or not. For legal purposes, however, Japan employs the “three signs of death” (shi no sanchoko) used by medical professionals: cardiac arrest, respiratory arrest, and loss of brainstem reflexes. If all three of these conditions are present at the same time and irreversible, then that person is deemed deceased.

Legal Insight says that zombies do exhibit the three signs of death, but I beg to differ. This is a problematic claim because there have been so many different zombie stories with zombies of wildly varying abilities, but even despite that, I don’t think any of them even exhibits one of the three signs of death, let alone all three.

Starting with cardiac arrest, zombies bleed when shot and clearly have muscle function, either of which would be impossible a beating heart. 

▼ Your Honor, if it pleases the court, I’d like to submit this gnarly video of Claire doming a couple zombies in Resident Evil 2 Remake. As you can clearly see from the blood spurting from their neckholes, they demonstrate arterial pressure which can only be achieved by a functioning heart.

And while they may not require it to function, zombies clearly breathe. How else do they make those “gnnnhhhurghhhh” noises? And brainstem reflexes? Baby, zombies are all about brainstem reflex.

▼ I’d now like to call Dr. Edwin Jenner of the CDC in the USA to the stand. He’ll explain to us that zombies have functioning brainstems beyond a shadow of a doubt.

So, whether it’s the ambling Night of the Living Dead zombies or your parkour-running 28 Days Later zombies, they are legally living humans and, as such, it could be argued that zombies would have rights in Japan. This means a cop or soldier cannot open fire on a zombie simply because they gave them a dirty look or even if they start walking towards them menacingly. The violence used against them must be in direct proportion to their own unlawful attack… which I guess means all soldiers can do is bite the zombies back.

So, in conclusion, the JSDF would be prohibited from gunning down zombies wholesale, and Japanese police would be legally obliged to arrest you for assault if one falls off the hood of your car while you drive away in a panic. That being said, in most zombie outbreaks the government seems to go down pretty quickly, and all laws just go out the window anyway.

Happy Halloween!

title: Guile cosplay goes with everyone for Halloween at SoraNews24 HQ [Photos]
description: Go home and be a family man? Nah, we have to go to work. We keep SoraNews24 HQ clean enough so that we don’t have flies on the wall, but if you were to be, for instance, a shapeshifting tanuki disguised as a fern in the corner of our office on Friday, you might have […]
content:
Go home and be a family man? Nah, we have to go to work.

We keep SoraNews24 HQ clean enough so that we don’t have flies on the wall, but if you were to be, for instance, a shapeshifting tanuki disguised as a fern in the corner of our office on Friday, you might have heard the following conversation take place.

Mr. Sato: “Hey, you guys bring your Guile gear?”

P.K.: “Yeah.”

Mr. Sato: “OK. So, we doing this?”

Ahiruneko: “We sure are. But, like, I really didn’t have much to bring.”

Mr. Sato: “But, like, -how- are we supposed to do this? We just, like, become Guile?”

Seiji Nakazawa: “Sure. No need to overthink it, right?”

P.K.: “We all just turn into Guile, just like that?”

See, we have a tradition here at SoraNews24, where everyone who’s in the office on the day closest to Halloween dresses up in costume. We try to have some sort of theme, like dressing up as the trendiest desert drink of the year or trying to transform into actual parts of the Tokyo cityscape. This year, we settled on the theme of developer Capcom’s hit fighting video game series, Street Fighter, and since every release since Street Fighter II: Championship Edition has allowed players to pick the same character as each other, we decided that everyone in the office would become Guile.

Mr. Sato: “I think everybody already has their outfit sorted, so we better get started on our making our Guile hair.”

Takeshi Harada: “How are we supposed to do that?”

Mr. Sato: “All you need is some yellow paper, and some imagination.”

With Hollywood’s newest live-action Street Fighter adaptation currently playing in theaters, some might be tempted to accuse us of trying to piggyback on the movie’s hype train, but our Guile-loving credentials have been an established matter of public record for some time, as we previously published a literally hard-hitting investigative piece on the real-world effectiveness of Guile’s iconically cool-looking low-guard pose from the games.

Takeshi: “Am I doing it right?”

Mr. Sato: “Hey, man, you gotta trust your own judgement when making Guile hair.”

Then, after 20 minutes of cutting, taping, and changing clothes in a wide-open office with no locker room…

Mr. Sato: “OK, everybody set? Show us your Guiles!”

So, uh, as you can see, even though everyone was dressed as the same character, there was still plenty of, let’s call them individual creative differences present in the final results.

Let’s take a closer look at what everyone came up with.

▼ Seiji Guile!

▼ Yuichiro Guile!

▼ Ahiruneko Guile!

▼ Takeshi Guile!

▼ P.K. Guile!

▼ Yoshio Guile!

▼ Sato Guile!

▼ Go Hatori Guile, who actually wasn’t in the office this day but who joined the battle via a photo taken ahead of time!

So who’s Guile was the best Guile? We left that judgement up to Seiji, since we felt like we kind of owed him one for all the physical punishment he took in that Guile blocking test.

Seiji Guile: “All right, you maggots! Line up for inspection!”

Seiji Guile: “Sato Guile! You are the sorriest display of a Guile in this whole company!”

Sato Guile: “What? But I thought I did pretty good. I even worked out extra to tone up my arms and shoulders for this.”

Seiji Guile: “I didn’t expect anything more of you than using paper for your hair, but why did you put the crease in the front? That’s inexcusable! You’re a disgrace to our proud Guile traditions!”

Seiji Guile: “Next! Yoshio Guile! You’re all right. I can tell you’re taking the mission seriously.”

Seiji Guile: “Unlike the rest of these knuckleheads who just used drawing paper, you reinforced your spikes with construction paper. That’s the kind of ingenuity that we need to be ready to display in the field.”

Yoshio Guile: “Sir! Thank you, sir!”

Seiji Guile: “Next! Ahiruneko Guile! What in the name of a redizzy combo do you call this?”

Ahiruneko Guile: “No good?”

Seiji Guile: “No good at all! That sloppy, loose tank top is totally outside uniform regulations!”

Ahiruneko Guile: “Well, I mean, I just bought it on Amazon, so it wasn’t like I could try it on and check the fit or anything…”

Seiji Guile: “You think Guile would be caught dead in something like that? You’re a disgrace to the uniform!”

Seiji Guile: “Next! P.K. Guile!”

P.K. Guile: “Look, I’ll just get it out of the way and apologize right now.”

Seiji Guile: “Well, at least you’ve got a scrap of self awareness. You know your pants are wrong, right?”

P.K. Guile: “When I went to the thrift shop, this was all they had for camo pants. I know the color is wrong.”

Seiji Guile: “No, actually Guile has alternate color versions with blue pants, so that’s not the problem. But what no one has ever seen is Guile rolling up his pants!”

Seiji Guile: “Next! Takeshi Guile!”

Seiji Guile: “You clearly didn’t understand the assignment either! A digital camouflage pattern? Seriously? You know Guile doesn’t wear that!”

Takeshi Guile: “I went to a thrift store too, and this was the only pair of camo pants I could find.”

Seiji Guile: “You’re endangering the whole mission by relying on thrift stores! Next time shop online if you need to and make sure you get the pattern right!”

Seiji Guile: “Next! Yuichiro Guile! Let’s wrap this up!”

Seiji Guile: “So tell me how you managed to forget you’re supposed to be Guile? You look like you just came from the kitchen or the beach!”

Seiji Guile: “That hairline’s crammed all the way down onto your eyebrows, like you’re wearing chef’s hat! And shorts? Shorts?!! How’re you gonna have a proper street fight without proper pants?”

Seiji Guile: “Aside from Yoshio and Go, none of you are ready to be Guile! Guess it’s up to me to whip you all into shape.”

Guiles: “Yes, sir!”

Seiji Guile: “ATTEN-TION! Company, form up and…flash kick charge pose!”

Guiles: “Yes, sir!”

Seiji Guile: “Crouching guard!”

Guiles: “Yes, sir!”

Seiji Guile: “Just you wait and see! I’ll turn you all into real Guiles yet!”

Parting is such very, very sweet sorrow.

No one’s really watching their calories on October 31, right? Between trick-or-treating, Halloween parties, and all those tempting candy displays in the stores, there’s no better occasion for indulging your sweet tooth multiple times during the same day. And if you’re already leaving room for desserts, this Halloween is a very good time to make a visit to Cold Stone, because on October 31 they’re permanently closing their last remaining branch in east Japan.

Cold Stone’s time in Japan has been a rollercoaster ride. The chain first showed up in Japan in 2005 and became an immediate sensation among sweets fans, with long lines forming to try the offerings of the American “creamery” and listening to the staff’s cheerful singing voices while they waited. For a while there, Cold Stone looked poised to enter the ranks of Japan’s lovingly adopted brands from the U.S. such as McDonald’s and Starbuck’s. Unfortunately, not long after Cold Stone Japan’s expansion plans heated up, consumer enthusiasm for the chain started to cool off. In time, branches started closing down, with the even vacating Tokyo entirely for a while.

Eventually, though, Cold Stone found its way back to the capital. In 2023, it opened a new branch Tokyo’s Tama district, and then another in downtown’s trendy Harajuku neighborhood.

▼ The Harajuku branch, shortly after its opening in June of 2023

Sadly, neither of those comeback bids panned out, and by April of 2025, there were once again no Cold Stone branches anywhere in Tokyo, and the only remaining location in all of east Japan was located inside an outlet shopping mall in Tochigi Prefecture…which closed down one month later.

But then this past summer came a ray of hope for Cold Stone fans in east Japan with the opening of a Cold Stone branch in the town of Kamakura in Kanagawa Prefecture, Tokyo’s neighbor to the south. Kamakura is a major sightseeing destination, with temples, shrines, hiking trails, and beaches, and it’s only about an hour by train from Tokyo, making it an easy daytrip for Tokyoites and travelers staying at hotels in the capital.

▼ Video of the Kamakura Cold Stone’s opening day on July 30

View this post on Instagram

Being a big Cold Stone fan, our ace reporter Mr. Sato was thrilled to have the chain back in east Japan, and was looking forward to getting a scoop or two the next time he was down in Kamakura. The urgency on his plans to visit the city got rapidly cranked up, though, when on October 29 Cold Stone Japan announced through its official Instagram account that it would be permanently closing its Kamakura branch, and doing so in just two days’ time, on October 31.

So Mr. Sato dropped everything, dashed to the station, and rode the train to Kamakura.

The Kamakura Cold Stone has a pretty good location. It’s outside JR Kamakura Station’s west exit, which isn’t as busy and developed as the east side of the structure, but there’s still a decent amount of foot traffic, especially since the shop is close to the transfer gates for the Enoden rail line that runs along the shore and provides ironically picturesque views.

At this point, Mr. Sato might still have been able to delude himself into believing that there’d been some kind of mistake in Cold Stone’s Instagram announcement, and that the store wasn’t actually shutting down after just three months in business. But sure enough, there was a written notice posted at the counter that said:

Cold Stone Creamery Kamakura Station
Notice of closure

We are grateful to the support shown by so many visitors since our opening. As of October 31, Cold Stone Creamery Kamakura Station will be closing.

We wish to take this opportunity to sincerely thank all of our customers. We will continue to do our best to provide all of you with Happy Creamery experiences.

We look forward to seeing all of your smiles again someday. Thank you so much for everything.

So this was really going to be goodbye. Carefully weighing his options for this final Cold Stone session, Mr. Sato asked for Dobai chocolate ice cream in a chocolate waffle bowl, covered with chocolate sauce. “Is it OK if we sing?” asked the staff, unwaveringly cheerful, even now, and Mr. Sato said “Yes! Please!”

“I was sad to hear you’ll be closing.” Said Mr. Sato after the song was finished and they handed him his order. “Yes, we only found out about it two days ago,” said the clerk, revealing that they’d apparently been as surprised as Mr. Sato was at the turn of events.

▼ Mr. Sato’s ice cream. He does not fool around when it comes to grand finales of his favorite dessert places.

Mr. Sato couldn’t help silently wondering why it had to end like this. It’s not like Japan doesn’t like ice cream. As a matter of fact, Japan loves ice cream. Baskin-Robbins has over 1,000 branches in Japan, including one on the other side of Kamakura Station. Aside from specialty shops, fast food chains and snack stands sell ice cream all year round, as do convenience stores and super markets.

So why can’t Cold Stone seem to get a stronger foothold in the country? The company hasn’t made any official statement explaining its woes, but as we’ve discussed before, it might have something to do with the kind of ice cream that Cold Stone serves not matching up with how Japan would like it served. Ice cream fans in Japan are fine with casual settings or eating on the go for simple frozen treats, like a modest-sized scoop of Baskin-Robbins or personal-size serving of Häagen-Dazs. On the other end of the spectrum, leisurely savoring a large, decadent parfait at a cozy or fashionable cafe is considered a highlight-of-the-day-caliber experience. Cold Stone, though, doesn’t really fit into either of those two scenarios. Their desserts are big, heavy, and potentially messy, the sort of thing that Japanese sweets fans usually want to sit down and take their time with, but Cold Stone’s focus has always been primarily on take-out, and that incongruent combination is likely a limiting factor in terms of the chain’s potential appeal to a broad demographic in Japan.

This does, though, leave the limited demographic of passionate Cold Stone fans like Mr. Sato in an unfortunate position, though, since even if they do exist, there apparently just aren’t enough of them to keep Cold Stone a viable venture. It’s enough to bring a tear to your eye…but after hearing the staff bravely sing as they put together his order, Mr. Sato knew that if he was going to have to say goodbye, again, he was going to say goodbye with a smile.

The October 31 closing means that, as of November 1, there will be only one remaining Cold Stone in all of Japan, located in the Mitsui Outlet Park Jazz Dream Nagashima in Mie Prefecture. Even taking the Shinkansen, it takes about three hours to get there from Tokyo, so Mr. Sato’s first wish would be for Cold Stone to rest up and make one more comeback attempt in the Tokyo area, but if they can’t, he might just need to book some bullet train tickets the next time his cravings hit.
